item.title: Identity and Access Architecture for Azure Landing Zones: Entra ID, RBAC, and PIM
item.description:
The security team’s Slack message arrives on a Tuesday afternoon: “We’re seeing resource deletions in prod. Investigating.” Your heart rate goes up. You pull the Azure Activity Log. The deletions are attributed to a service principal—one your team created eight months ago for a deployment pipeline. The pipeline finished its job. Nobody revoked the credential. The client secret was valid for two years.

It wasn’t a sophisticated attack. Someone found the secret in a Git history, and the principal had Contributor on the entire subscription. Everything it could touch, they touched.

item.title: The Enterprise Case: Security and Privacy with Local AI
item.description:
Your team completes a three-month migration to an air-gapped environment to satisfy new compliance requirements. Two security audits. Significant budget. Two weeks after go-live, someone discovers the developers are using personal phone hotspots to access GitHub Copilot — because the local alternatives weren’t fast enough and nobody provisioned one.

Shadow AI is not a behavior problem. It’s an infrastructure gap. And it’s a harder compliance violation than the one you just spent three months fixing.

item.title: Expression Security: Preventing Injection and Hardening Your YAML
item.description:
“Enter your environment name: prod; rm -rf /”. If that input reached your pipeline, would it crash your production server? Most DevOps engineers worry about network firewalls and SSH keys, but they leave a massive back door open: Expression Injection. In the rush to build “dynamic” pipelines, we often blindly trust user-provided parameters and runtime variables, turning our YAML into an execution engine for malicious actors.

Azure DevOps expressions are not just for logic; they are interpolation engines. When you use the macro syntax ($( )) without sanitization, you are performing a raw string replacement on a shell script. A malicious user can provide a value that “escapes” the intended command, allowing them to steal secrets, modify source code, or bypass deployment approvals. Here are the mechanics of expression injection and the patterns for hardening your YAML logic using typed parameters and safe ingestion.

item.title: Security Baseline: Defender for Cloud and Microsoft Sentinel in a Landing Zone
item.description:
The compliance report lands in your inbox on a Tuesday morning. One finding: a production subscription had diagnostic logs disabled for 47 days. No one noticed because no one was watching. The subscription was vended six weeks ago, the app team started deploying workloads a week after that, and somewhere in between, the security coverage that was supposed to be automatic… wasn’t.

That gap — between “we have a landing zone” and “we have a landing zone with security built in” — is where incidents live.

item.title: How One Forgotten Pipeline Secret Deleted Production
item.description:
Tuesday, 2:22 PM. The patient portal returns errors on every page, and the security channel has one message in it: “Seeing resource deletions in production. Investigating.” You open the Activity Log for rg-portal-prod and watch the list scroll. The App Service. The Function App. The SQL database. The Key Vault. Forty-one delete operations between 2:05 and 2:19. Fourteen minutes.

The caller column doesn’t show an employee, and it doesn’t show an account anyone would call an attacker’s. It shows sp-portal-deploy, a service principal your team created in February for a GitHub Actions workflow that was deleted in April. The pipeline is gone. The identity, its Contributor role on the subscription, and its two-year client secret are not.

item.title: The Best 7B and 8B Code Models in 2026, and Which Ones Security Will Approve
item.description:
Your head of platform forwards a one-line email from the CISO: “Can we run a code model ourselves instead of sending source code to a vendor?” You already know the shortlist. You’ve read the benchmarks, pulled a couple of models into Ollama on your workstation, and watched one of them write a decent Terraform module in four seconds.

Then you start drafting the answer and realize the benchmarks cover the part nobody on the approval committee will ask about. They’ll ask who trained the model, under what license, where the weights came from, what happens to the code you feed it, and who can reach the server it runs on. “It scored well on HumanEval” doesn’t answer any of those.
